title: The Sharpe Pint: Hormuz Carrots, Bond Vigilantes, and the Human Moat

opening_mood.text: Happy Friday, team. Grab a flat white and pull up a chair. Today, we are looking at a massive diplomatic carrot from Iran that has temporarily cooled the oil market, a bond market that is still terrorising real estate valuations, and why the ultimate career moat in the age of LLMs might actually be... learning how to talk to people. Let's dive in.

content.text: It has been a frantic 24 hours across global markets, with geopolitical chess in New York, high-stakes trade diplomacy in Washington, and some serious structural shifts in the bond markets. Here is what you need to know to look smart in your morning meetings.
1. Iran's Hormuz Carrot: A Seven-Day Reopening Proposal

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi dropped a bombshell on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York, proposing a step-by-step plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days. The catch? The US must lift its naval blockade and halt regional hostilities, including those in Lebanon. On the news, Brent crude pulled back by roughly 2%, dipping below the 100-dollar mark to trade around 99 dollars a barrel as traders weighed the potential for a diplomatic breakthrough.

Why it matters: The Strait of Hormuz is the absolute jugular of global energy transit, carrying about a fifth of the world's oil. The blockade and subsequent energy shock have been the primary drivers keeping global inflation sticky and central banks hawkish. A genuine reopening would dramatically ease supply-side inflation pressures, but the Trump administration has already signalled it will not easily return to previous ceasefire terms.

The City angle: For macro traders and asset managers, this is the ultimate binary event. If the deal goes through, we could see a massive relief rally in equities and a sharp drop in energy costs. If it falls apart, we are locked into a structural energy shock. Keep a close eye on the oil-to-bond yield transmission mechanism over the coming days.

items: What to say at work: It is a massive diplomatic carrot, but the White House is highly unlikely to accept the old June ceasefire terms without squeezing Tehran for major concessions first.

What to say in an interview: The Hormuz blockade is the single biggest supply-side risk to global inflation. Even a temporary reopening would give the Fed and the ECB some much-needed breathing room to pause their current rate-hiking cycles.

content.text: 2. Global Bond Selloff Pauses, but Yields Hover Near Multi-Year Highs

The brutal global bond selloff took a brief breather on Friday, but sovereign yields remain anchored near their highest levels in nearly two decades. The US 10-year Treasury yield eased slightly to around 5.18% after flirting with 5.23% on Thursday, while the 30-year yield remains stubbornly close to 5.5%. The selloff has been fuelled by a resilient US economy, persistent inflation, and the Federal Reserve's recent 25-basis-point rate hike to a 3.75% to 4.00% range under new Chair Kevin Warsh.

Why it matters: Higher yields increase borrowing costs across the entire economy, squeeze equity valuations (especially long-duration tech stocks), and make corporate refinancing incredibly expensive. The market is rapidly pricing in a structural shift where the risk-free rate is no longer a cosy baseline, but a high hurdle that risky assets must work hard to clear.

The City angle: For quants and asset allocators, the traditional equity risk premium is looking incredibly thin. Private credit funds, which thrived in the low-rate era, are also facing a reality check as their portfolio companies struggle with deteriorating interest coverage ratios.

items: What to say at work: We are looking at a structural repricing of the risk-free rate. If you are pitching a deal or running a valuation model, the WACC assumptions we used even twelve months ago are completely obsolete.

What to say in an interview: The combination of resilient economic growth and persistent energy-driven inflation means the neutral rate of interest is likely much higher than central banks previously estimated. This structurally alters long-term asset allocation.

content.text: 3. Trump and Xi Extend Tariff Truce at Washington Summit

During Chinese President Xi Jinping's high-stakes state visit to Washington, the US and China agreed to extend their bilateral tariff truce until January 10, 2027. The truce, which keeps tariff rates stable, was originally set to expire on November 10. While the extension avoids an immediate trade war, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent noted that major disagreements remain, particularly regarding incomplete Chinese purchases of US agricultural products and advanced AI technology export controls.

Why it matters: A renewed trade war between the world's two largest economies would have sent shockwaves through global supply chains and exacerbated global inflation. The extension provides a tactical pause, but it does not resolve the deep-seated strategic competition over technology, Taiwan, and Beijing's geopolitical alignments.

The City angle: This is a classic kick-the-can exercise. Trump is keeping the tariff threat alive as leverage ahead of the G20 summit in Miami this December. For multinational corporates and supply chain analysts, the threat of a hard tariff wall in early 2027 remains a major tail risk that must be hedged.

items: What to say at work: The tariff truce extension is classic Trump. He is keeping the leverage, kicking the can to January, and waiting to see what Xi brings to the table in Miami. It is short-term relief for retail and tech supply chains, but nobody is unpacking their bags just yet.

What to say in an interview: The extension prevents a short-term stagflationary shock, but the underlying trend of economic decoupling and technology balkanisation between the US and China remains fully intact.

content.text: 4. Starbucks to Shut 250 North American Stores in Portfolio Shake-up

Starbucks has announced plans to close approximately 250 underperforming coffeehouses in North America later this week, representing about 1% of its regional footprint. The decision is part of its Back to Starbucks turnaround strategy, which focuses on operational efficiency, speed of service, and margin protection, even as the broader North American business returns to growth.

Why it matters: In a high-inflation, high-wage environment, brick-and-mortar retail giants can no longer afford to carry underperforming locations. Starbucks is aggressively pruning its portfolio to focus on high-performing, upgraded stores that can consistently deliver on its new service standards.

The City angle: Equity research analysts love this kind of operational discipline. Instead of chasing raw store-count growth to please the market, Starbucks is prioritising unit economics and capital allocation efficiency. It is a clear sign that corporate America is shifting its focus from top-line expansion to bottom-line resilience.

items: What to say at work: Starbucks closing 1% of its stores while reporting overall growth shows they are serious about margin discipline. It is a textbook case of prioritising return on invested capital over vanity footprint metrics.

What to say in an interview: In a high-cost environment, corporate strategy must pivot from aggressive footprint expansion to density and unit-level profitability. Starbucks is executing this playbook perfectly.

content.text: 5. Rocket Lab Stockholders Approve Historic Iridium Acquisition

Iridium Communications stockholders overwhelmingly approved the company's acquisition by Rocket Lab, with 99.6% of votes cast in favor of the merger. Rocket Lab has already fully funded the cash portion of the 1.94-billion-dollar deal through a massive At-The-Market equity offering, marking a major milestone toward creating a vertically integrated space powerhouse.

Why it matters: This is one of the most transformative M&A deals in the space sector. By combining Rocket Lab's launch and satellite manufacturing capabilities with Iridium's global satellite communications network and rare spectrum, the combined entity becomes a tier-1 space power capable of challenging SpaceX's dominance.

The City angle: Space is no longer just a venture capital playground; it is consolidating into institutional-grade infrastructure. Rocket Lab's ability to successfully pull off a nearly 2-billion-dollar equity raise to fund a major acquisition shows deep public market liquidity and investor appetite for high-conviction space plays.

items: What to say at work: Rocket Lab buying Iridium is a massive vertical integration play. They are no longer just launching other people's hardware; they now own the network, the spectrum, and the cash flow. It is the closest thing the public markets have to a viable competitor to Starlink.

What to say in an interview: This deal highlights the transition of the space economy from speculative venture capital to mature, cash-generative M&A. It proves that vertical integration is the winning strategy in high-cost, capital-intensive industries.

content.text: 6. Corteva's Spinoff of Vylor Approved by SEC

Corteva announced that the SEC has declared effective the Form 10 registration statement for the spinoff of its seed and genetics business, Vylor Inc. The tax-free distribution is scheduled to complete on October 1, 2026, with Vylor set to begin regular-way trading on the NYSE under the ticker VYLR.

Why it matters: Corteva is splitting into two pure-play entities: Vylor, which will focus on advanced seeds, genetics, and AI-driven gene-editing, and Corteva, which will focus on crop protection and specialty chemicals. Vylor is being positioned as a high-margin business targeting a 30% EBITDA margin.

The City angle: Spinoffs are a favourite hunting ground for event-driven hedge funds. By separating the high-multiple, IP-heavy seed business from the more cyclical crop protection business, the transaction aims to unlock significant shareholder value and eliminate the conglomerate discount.

items: What to say at work: The Corteva/Vylor split is a classic sum-of-the-parts story. Vylor is the high-margin, IP-heavy seed business that should command a premium multiple, especially with their new AI-driven gene-editing partnerships. It is definitely one for the event-driven book.

What to say in an interview: Corporate breakups like this show that management teams are under pressure to simplify business models. Pure-play entities are much easier for the market to value and typically attract a more targeted investor base.

sections.title: Markets Briefing: What Moved and Why

content.text: If you are heading to the pub this evening, the market chat is simple: bonds are still eating the world, but a diplomatic olive branch in the Middle East has given equities a Friday morning breather. After a volatile week where fixed income traders looked like they were trying to break their screens, we are seeing a classic 'pause and reflect' session. Equities are nudging higher, oil is cooling, and the relentless march of yields has temporarily stalled.

Let's start with the elephant in the room: the bond market. On Thursday, the US 10-year Treasury yield hit a multi-decade high of 5.23%, a level not seen since the summer of 2007, while the 30-year yield touched 5.50%. This was not a random drift. It was driven by a toxic cocktail of hawkish central bank rhetoric—with the Fed's John Williams hinting at more hikes and the ECB's Isabel Schnabel warning of spreading price pressures—combined with hot PMI data and a disastrously weak 70 billion dollar five-year Treasury auction. Fixed income investors are demanding serious compensation to hold long-term debt, and the market is now pricing in a 70% chance of another Fed hike in October.

Why does this matter for your asset allocation models? Here is a killer stat for your next team meeting: the 10-year US Treasury yield has officially crossed above the US single-family rental cap rate (currently around 4.8%) for the first time in over 20 years. Think about the plumbing of that. Buying real estate for cash flow now has a negative opportunity cost compared to risk-free government paper. When you can clip a 5.2% coupon from Uncle Sam with zero operational hassle, the hurdle rate for every other asset class—from private equity to commercial property—goes through the roof. This is not just a blip; it is a fundamental regime shift.

Over in commodities, oil has been behaving like a geopolitical yo-yo. Brent crude spiked past 106 dollars a barrel on Thursday after Yemen's Houthi rebels claimed successful missile and drone strikes on Saudi Aramco facilities in Yanbu and Riyadh. However, Brent eased back to around 105.50 dollars on Friday morning following reports of back-channel US-Iran diplomacy at the UN General Assembly. Qatari mediators are reportedly working on a phased deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz—which is currently seeing just 12 transits a day compared to its pre-war average of 140—in exchange for easing the US naval blockade. If a truce lands, it could take a massive inflation premium out of the energy complex.

Meanwhile, the geopolitical theatre in Washington was peak Trump. The US President hosted Chinese President Xi Jinping for a lavish state dinner featuring sesame-crusted sea bass and a guest list packed with tech royalty, including Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos, and OpenAI's Greg Brockman. The headline result? The key tariff truce has been extended to January 10. Underneath the glitz, Xi used his speech to warn against the 'Thucydides trap' and called for 'human control' over AI. It is a fascinating dynamic: even as the two superpowers clash over technology and trade, they are desperate to keep the lines open to prevent a hard economic landing.

To round up the board: Wall Street ended Thursday virtually flat, with the S&P 500 at 7,704.13 and the Nasdaq at 26,939.37, while the Dow slipped 0.3%. On Friday morning, European markets are enjoying the respite, with the FTSE 100 up 0.5% to 10,733.65 and the DAX gaining 1.0%. In FX, the yen remains under severe pressure, keeping Tokyo on high intervention alert despite Trump grumbling to Japan's PM Takaichi about the weak currency. Bitcoin is holding its ground, trading quietly around 84,160 dollars. Enjoy your weekend pints, but keep one eye on the Treasury screens—the bond vigilantes are far from finished.

content.text: The Fulcrum Security: Holding the Keys to the Corporate Kingdom

When a company is sliding towards administration or Chapter 11, its equity is usually toast. But a fascinating game of musical chairs begins in the capital structure. The senior bank lenders are safe, but in the middle lies the 'fulcrum security'—the holy grail for distressed debt and special situations investors.

In plain English, the fulcrum security is the specific class of debt that is only partially covered by the company's actual assets or enterprise value (often called the 'value break'). Because there isn't enough cash to pay them back in full, but too much value for them to be wiped out completely, this debt class ends up being swapped for the lion's share of the company's equity during a restructuring. If you own the fulcrum security, you effectively own the post-bankruptcy company.
A Pub-Friendly Example
Let's say 'GastroPubs Ltd' has hit the wall. Its enterprise value (EV) has collapsed from £1bn to £500m. Here is how its capital structure looks:

items: Senior Secured Bank Debt: £300m
Junior Mezzanine Debt: £300m
Unsecured Bonds: £200m
Equity: £100m (nominally, but practically worthless)

content.text: If we distribute the £500m of actual value down the waterfall: The senior lenders get their £300m in full. That leaves £200m of value. The mezzanine lenders are owed £300m, but there is only £200m left for them. They are the fulcrum security. They won't get paid in cash; instead, they will swap their debt for 100% of the new equity in the restructured GastroPubs Ltd. The unsecured bondholders and the original equity holders get absolutely nothing—wiped out.
Why It Matters in the City

Distressed debt heavyweights like Oaktree, Apollo, or SVP Global don't just buy debt for the coupon. They play a game called 'loan-to-own'. They will quietly buy up the mezzanine debt on the secondary market at a massive discount—say, 40 pence on the pound. Once the company defaults, they use their blocking position in that fulcrum class to push for a debt-for-equity swap. Suddenly, they've acquired a £500m business for a fraction of the cost, clean of its old debt burden.
The Classic Schoolboy Error

The most common mistake is chasing the highest 'yield' or the cheapest paper. Retail investors or junior analysts often look at the unsecured bonds trading at 5p on the pound and think, 'If this company survives, I'll make 20x!' But in a restructuring, the waterfall is absolute. If the value stops at the mezzanine level, the unsecured bonds are legally extinguished. Cheap debt is cheap for a reason; if it's below the fulcrum, it's just a lottery ticket where the draw has already happened.
How to Ace This in an Interview
If you are interviewing for a restructuring investment banking role, a distressed debt hedge fund, or a special situations private equity desk, this is bread-and-butter stuff.

If asked how you would evaluate a distressed company, don't just talk about DCFs. Say: 'I'd first estimate the restructured enterprise value, then build a debt waterfall to identify the fulcrum security. That's where the real valuation tension and the opportunity to take control of the equity lies.'
Over a Pint: What to Say

"Everyone is looking at the equity slide, but the real action is in the junior notes. At 45 cents on the dollar, they are the clear fulcrum security. If we get a debt-for-equity swap, we're buying the operating business at a 4.0x EBITDA multiple once the balance sheet is cleaned up."

sections.title: Quant / AI Finance Idea of the Day

content.text: If you have ever built a machine learning model to predict stock returns, you have probably run into the classic 'garbage in, garbage out' problem of portfolio optimisation. You feed your neural network's shiny point-estimate predictions into a standard Markowitz mean-variance optimiser, and it immediately tells you to put 95% of your capital into three highly volatile small-cap stocks because it predicted a massive return. The optimiser is completely oblivious to the fact that those predictions have a massive margin of error.

Usually, quants patch this by slapping an L1 penalty (Lasso) onto the portfolio weights to force sparsity and prevent overfitting. It works, but it has always felt like a bit of a heuristic hack—a machine learning band-aid rather than proper financial theory. However, a paper by Yuan Liao, Xinjie Ma, Andreas Neuhierl, and Linda Schilling provides a beautiful, mathematically rigorous economic justification for this exact practice.
The Idea: Lasso as Uncertainty Aversion

The authors show that if you model an investor who is uncertainty-averse (in the classical Knightian sense) and wants to maximise their worst-case expected return within a confidence interval around the ML model's predictions, the resulting max-min optimisation problem is mathematically identical to an adaptive Lasso-penalised portfolio optimisation. In other words, Lasso is not just a machine learning trick; it is the exact mathematical behaviour of a rational investor who does not fully trust their own model.
The Math in Action

Instead of taking the predicted returns as gospel, the uncertainty-averse investor defines a Forecast Confidence Interval (FCI) around each prediction: [predicted_return - q, predicted_return + q], where q is proportional to the standard error of the prediction. They then solve for the portfolio that performs best under the worst-case scenario within those intervals. The paper proves this max-min problem collapses into a single-step minimisation:
Minimize: 0.5 * gamma * w^T * Sigma * w - w^T * mu_hat + sum( q_i * |w_i| )

Where gamma is risk aversion, Sigma is the covariance matrix, mu_hat is the vector of predicted returns, and the penalty on each asset's weight w_i is scaled exactly by q_i—the uncertainty of its prediction. If a stock's predicted return is high but its standard error is massive, the penalty shrinks its weight to exactly zero. This creates a natural 'non-participation' region for assets where the model is just guessing.
Python Implementation
Here is how you can set up and solve this uncertainty-averse portfolio using cvxpy, translating prediction standard errors directly into adaptive Lasso penalties:

import cvxpy as cp
import numpy as np

def solve_uncertainty_averse_portfolio(mu_hat, sigma, std_errors, gamma=2.0, eta=1.5):
    """
    Solves the Uncertainty-Averse Mean-Variance Portfolio (UA-MV).
    Equivalent to an adaptive Lasso-penalised mean-variance optimisation.
    """
    n = len(mu_hat)
    w = cp.Variable(n)
    q = eta * std_errors
    portfolio_variance = cp.quad_form(w, sigma)
    expected_return = w @ mu_hat
    lasso_penalty = cp.norm1(cp.multiply(q, w))
    objective = cp.Minimize(0.5 * gamma * portfolio_variance - expected_return + lasso_penalty)
    constraints = [cp.sum(w) == 1.0]
    prob = cp.Problem(objective, constraints)
    prob.solve()
    return w.value
How to Use This in an Interview or at the Pub

items: The Interview Question: "How do you handle the sensitivity of mean-variance portfolios to input errors?"
The Standard Answer: "You can use Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage on the covariance matrix, or use Black-Litterman to anchor the returns."

The Smart Answer: "Actually, there is a beautiful paper by Liao et al. (2025) that shows Lasso regularisation on portfolio weights is the exact mathematical dual of Knightian uncertainty aversion. If you optimise for the worst-case return within the confidence interval of your ML predictions, the math collapses into an adaptive Lasso where the penalty on each asset is its forecast standard error. It gives a solid economic foundation to why we regularise weights, rather than just treating it as a machine learning heuristic."

sources.title: The Uncertainty of Machine Learning Predictions in Asset Pricing
sources.note: This paper establishes the asymptotic distribution of neural network forecasts in asset pricing and proves the equivalence between uncertainty-averse portfolio selection and adaptive Lasso regularisation.

sections.title: One Article or Paper Worth Reading

content.text: The Human Premium in a Machine World

If you spend your days in the City, you have likely spent the last couple of years looking over your shoulder at LLMs, wondering if your coding, data-wrangling, or financial modelling skills are about to be automated into oblivion. That is why this week's pick is so refreshing. It is a short, sharp article titled 'In the Age of AI, A Quant's Edge is Human,' co-authored by David G. Kabiller (Co-founder of AQR Capital Management) and Francesca Cornelli (Dean of Kellogg School of Management), published on 10 September 2026.

Why this one? Because it comes from the absolute pinnacle of systematic, data-driven investing. When a firm built on hard mathematics, factor models, and massive computing power tells you that the future of quantitative finance is actually about emotional intelligence and creativity, you should probably put down your Python textbook and pay attention. It completely reframes how you should think about your own career moat in the City.
The Core Argument

The authors argue that while the investment industry has historically competed on raw analytical horsepower and technical skills, AI is rapidly turning these capabilities into cheap commodities. When everyone has access to models that can write clean code, run regressions, and parse earnings transcripts in seconds, technical execution ceases to be a competitive advantage. Instead, the durable differentiators will be things that cannot be easily automated:

items: Creativity: The ability to reframe intractable problems, design novel tests, and ask the questions that AI would never think to ask.
Emotional Intelligence (EQ): The capacity to lead, translate inscrutable complexity into clear solutions for clients, and build high-trust cultures.
Empathy in Leadership: The understanding of what motivates people, ensuring they do not feel like replaceable cogs in a machine.

content.text: To meet this shift, AQR is expanding its own internal 'Quanta Academy' (originally set up in 2015) to focus heavily on these non-replicable human skills. They are doubling down on their people as their ultimate competitive edge.
Key Takeaways

items: Technical skills are transitioning from a differentiator to mere table stakes.
AI is only as inspired as the humans directing it.
Empathy and leadership are not soft, fluffy concepts; they are hard economic drivers of talent retention and client trust.

content.text: The Choice Quotes

"AI is only as inspired as the humans who direct it, so the firms that lead the next era will be equally, if not more, focused on developing the human factor as they are on keeping pace with ever-advancing technology."
"We have seen too many brilliant analysts fail as leaders—not because their thinking was wrong, but because they could not get their people fully on board."
What to Skim vs. What to Read

You can skim the background on Kellogg's MBAi programme and the academic research on empathy. Focus your attention on the direct implications for how a top-tier hedge fund like AQR is changing its internal training and what they expect from their future leaders. That is where the real career gold is.
How It Connects to You

If you are an early-career analyst, associate, or VP, this is a massive green light to stop obsessing solely over your technical toolkit. Yes, you need to know how to use the tools, but your long-term career leverage lies in your ability to communicate, manage clients, and lead teams. The technical stuff is getting cheaper by the day; the ability to read the room as well as the balance sheet is where the premium is.
What to Say at the Pub or in an Interview

Try dropping this into your next work conversation or interview: 'I was reading a piece by David Kabiller at AQR, and it is fascinating how even the most hardcore systematic fund is doubling down on EQ. They are basically saying that when AI commoditises coding and data cleaning, the real alpha is just going to be human creativity and the ability to translate complex models into clear client solutions. It makes you think we should spend less time arguing over python libraries and more time learning how to actually manage people and build trust.'
The Sharpe Pint Take

It is easy to dismiss this kind of talk as corporate fluff when it comes from a retail bank, but coming from AQR—a firm that literally pioneered systematic factor investing—it carries serious weight. It is a healthy reminder that in finance, the final bottleneck is almost always human. A model is useless if you cannot convince a client to trust it during a drawdown, and a brilliant strategy is worthless if your team burns out and quits because of toxic management. The future belongs to the quants who can actually talk to people.

content.text: The Winner’s Curse: Why Winning a Bidding War Means You’ve Probably Lost

Picture this: you’re at a charity auction in a pub in the City, and there’s a giant jar of pound coins on the table. Everyone is invited to bid on it. The highest bid wins the jar. You get competitive, the adrenaline kicks in, you throw in a bid of £45, and boom—the hammer falls. You’ve won! You eagerly count the coins, only to find there’s exactly £32.40 in the jar. You are now the proud owner of a £12.60 loss, and a room full of colleagues who think you’re a genius.

This isn’t just a bad night at the pub; it’s a classic demonstration of The Winner’s Curse. First identified in 1971 by three petroleum engineers who noticed oil companies were consistently overpaying for drilling rights in the Gulf of Mexico, the concept was later popularised in behavioural economics by Richard Thaler.
The Mechanics of the Curse

The psychology of the curse is simple but brutal. In any competitive bidding situation where the asset has an objective, intrinsic value that is hard to pin down (what economists call a 'common value' auction), different bidders will estimate different values. Some will underestimate it, some will get it spot on, and some will wildly overestimate it.

Here’s the catch: the winner of the auction isn’t the person with the most accurate estimate. The winner is, by definition, the person with the highest estimate. And if the average estimate is roughly correct, the highest estimate is almost certainly too high. Therefore, the moment you win, you receive a piece of devastating information: everyone else in the room thought this thing was worth less than you did.
In the Wild: M&A and Talent Wars

In finance, the Winner’s Curse is the ghost that haunts the M&A department. Take the legendary case of Quaker Oats buying Snapple in 1993. In a highly competitive bidding war, Quaker snapped up the beverage brand for a cool $1.7 billion. Just 27 months later, having realised they couldn't extract the synergies they'd promised, they sold it to Triarc for $300 million. They paid a $1.4 billion premium for the privilege of winning.
We see this in everyday City life too:

items: The Talent War: Bidding frantically to hire a 'star' portfolio manager or quant. If you have to pay 40% over their current package to beat out three other funds, you’ve likely priced them at absolute perfection. If they turn out to be merely 'very good' rather than 'messianic', you’ve lost.

The VC Land Grab: Fighting to get into a hot Series A round. When five funds are competing, the valuation gets driven up to a level where the company has to become a literal unicorn just for you to break even.

content.text: How to Beat the Curse
If you want to avoid being the sucker at the table, you need to build structural speed bumps into your decision-making:

items: Distinguish Private vs. Common Value: If you are buying a painting because you love looking at it, that’s a 'private value' asset. There is no curse—if you pay £5,000 and love it, you won. But if you are buying a portfolio of non-performing loans, that’s a 'common value' asset. The value is purely financial, and the curse is active. Treat them differently.

Practice 'Bid Shading': This is the rational antidote. If your model says a target company is worth £100m, you must bid less than £100m. You have to discount your bid to account for the fact that if you actually win, your model was probably the most optimistic one out there.

The 'Pre-Commitment' Rule: Set your absolute walk-away price in the cold, hard light of day, before the bidding starts. Write it down. When the competitive arousal of the live auction kicks in and your boss whispers 'just one more bid', you point to the paper and walk.

content.text: One Line to Remember
In a bidding war, the winner is often the person who was most wrong.
